articles.title: Priscilla Chan's housing philanthropy helped finance 4,400 homes and protect 73,000 tenants in 5 years
articles.summary: Priscilla Chan has supported thousands of Bay Area residents through the ‘Partnership for the Bay’s Future,’ a programme created to tackle the region’s
articles.body: Priscilla Chan has supported thousands of Bay Area residents through the ‘Partnership for the Bay’s Future,’ a programme created to tackle the region’s shortage of affordable homes. 5 years after its launch, the initiative had protected more than 73,000 tenants and financed over 4,400 homes for thousands of people. The work, supported by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative(CZI), combines funding with policy support and partnerships involving governments, non-profits, developers and community groups. Its progress shows how philanthropic money can be used alongside other resources to address housing problems.Priscilla Chan’s philanthropy financed 4,000+ homes and protected over 70,000 tenantsThe Partnership for the Bay’s Future(PBF) began in 2019 with a focus on making housing more affordable while supporting racial equity and economic inclusion. According to the CZI’s April 2024 report on the partnership, its first 5 years resulted in more than 73,000 tenants being protected and more than 4,400 homes being financed for 11,000 people.According to the same report, community groups had helped bring the experiences of renters, low-income residents and people of colour into discussions with local, regional and state governments. More than 20,000 community members were engaged through policies connected to this work.The results came through 2 main parts of the partnership. First is policy work and second is housing finance. Instead of relying on a single programme, PBF created different ways to support people who were already living in the region while also helping produce and preserve affordable homes.PBF used flexible funding and community-led policy workOne part of PBF is its Policy Fund, which provides resources and technical assistance to local and regional governments. The aim is to help officials develop and put into practice policies that can allow more people to remain in their communities.The CZI reported that 36 policies had been proposed through the effort by April 2024, with 13 having passed. Examples included Berkeley’s Preference Policy and Antioch’s Cottage Communities on Faith-Owned Land.CZI reported in May 2024 that California’s housing shortage cannot be addressed through one measure alone and described the need for collaboration between activists, organisers, non-profits, philanthropies, private companies and community members. It also stressed that housing solutions can take time to produce results because the problem has developed over decades.What role did Chan Zuckerberg Initiative funding playThe housing finance side of PBF was designed to help close funding gaps that can prevent affordable housing projects from moving forward. Its ‘Family of Loan Funds’ supports the production and preservation of affordable homes across 5 Bay Area counties.By 2024, the loan funds had raised nearly $600 million and facilitated more than $404 million in investments. Those investments financed more than 4,400 homes. According to CZI, 90% of the units were intended for households earning 80% of the area median income or less, while half were for households at or below 50% of that level.CZI was an early investor, providing $50 million in initial capital. The organisation described that money as low-cost and risk-tolerant funding, which helped bring other funders into the housing effort. The loan funds are managed by the ‘Local Initiatives Support Corporation Bay Area’ and are intended to bridge financing gaps in the region’s rental housing market.Why affordable housing requires more than building new homesCZI also reports about several ways through which California can address affordability. One involves newer construction methods such as modular and panelised building, which can potentially reduce costs and shorten construction times. Another involves alternative forms of ownership, including community land trusts, housing co-operatives and resident-owned communities.The organisation also highlights the importance of protecting homes that are already affordable. Existing lower-cost rental properties can be lost when rents rise or buildings change ownership, leaving residents at risk of displacement. In Los Angeles, for example, CZI highlighted the Local Rental Owners Collaborative, which works with smaller landlords to help preserve housing and keep residents in their homes.Building more homes can increase supply, while preserving existing properties and protecting tenants can address immediate pressures on people already living in expensive areas.PBF’s 5-year experience is a model to tackle housing challengesThe April 2024 announcement described PBF as one of the largest private-sector housing funds focused on the Bay Area’s affordability crisis.At the 5-year mark, the partnership had not only financed thousands of homes but also supported policies affecting tenants across the region.Priscilla Chan has also described philanthropy as a relatively small part of a housing problem of this scale. According to the CZI report, the organisation saw a need for flexible approaches that could add to existing affordable housing support rather than replace it. The PBF reached its fifth anniversary in 2024. Its experience has since been presented as a model that other regions could consider adapting to their own housing challenges.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pakistan-administered Kashmir votes for president amid unrest
articles.summary: Lawmakers will choose a president despite seven vacant seats in districts at the centre of months of unrest.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Legislators in Pakistan-administered Kashmir are voting on Thursday to elect a president, filling the region’s last vacant constitutional office nearly eight months after the post fell vacant, well beyond the deadline set by its constitution.

Najeeb Naqi Khan, the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) candidate, is expected to win.

The party and its allies hold 32 of the 46 occupied seats in the 53-member Legislative Assembly, five more than the 27 votes required. The Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) holds 14.

But questions surrounding months of deadly unrest persist, as seven seats remain vacant because two districts at the centre of the protest movement have yet to vote.

Members of the region’s legislative assembly vote at the assembly secretariat in Muzaffarabad between 10am and 1pm local time.

Under the interim constitution, the president is elected by a majority of the assembly’s total membership, meaning 27 votes, regardless of how many seats are occupied.

The PMLN-backed Khan, 62, is a former member of the assembly from Palandri in Sudhnoti district, where he has won multiple elections. He has held several ministerial portfolios.

The PPP has nominated Chaudhry Latif Akbar, 78, a former assembly speaker who served as acting president from January until August.

Under the constitution, the president cannot be a member of the assembly.

Why has the office been vacant since January?

President Sultan Mehmood Chaudhry died in Islamabad on January 31, aged 71. He had been elected in 2021 on a Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) ticket. The PTI is led by former Prime Minister Imran Khan, who has been jailed for more than three years, but remains the country’s most popular politician.

The region’s constitution requires the speaker to have an election held within 30 days of the office falling vacant.

The speaker at the time was the PPP’s Akbar, who was also performing the president’s functions. No election was held.

In late February, a petition was filed at the region’s High Court for directions to hold the vote, naming the speaker, the chief election commissioner and the Election Commission among the respondents. The election still did not take place.

“Legally, according to the constitution, they should have held the presidential election. But because the federal government at the time was PMLN’s, they had it delayed,” alleged Ershad Mahmud, author of the book, Poonch: Identity, Politics and Resistance.

“Their calculation was that their own government would eventually form in AJK, so they’d be able to install their own president, and that’s precisely what happened. Otherwise, constitutionally, there’s no real justification for that delay,” the analyst who specialises in Kashmir affairs added.

The region’s legislative election was held in three phases on July 27, August 2 and August 10.

Polling in seven of the 11 constituencies in Poonch division was postponed before the final phase, including five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti.

Six weeks later, no new date has been set.

“So far, no dates have been given for polls in the constituencies where election was not possible due to security situation,” Chief Election Commissioner Justice (retd) Ghulam Mustafa Mughal told Al Jazeera. “We need safety and security to be priority.”

The PMLN won 25 of the 38 directly contested seats, while the PPP won 12. The PMLN also won six of eight reserved seats. Turnout was 48 percent, down from 61 percent in 2021.

The Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee, a popular grassroots umbrella organisation, was banned on June 5 under antiterrorism legislation.

Its central demand is the abolition of 12 seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees living elsewhere in Pakistan, which it says allow outsiders to shape the territory’s politics.

Internet services were cut across the region the same day. Broadband was restored on September 13 after 99 days, although mobile data remained restricted in parts of the region.

Residents and rights groups put the death toll from the unrest at more than 50. The government has not issued an overall figure but says at least seven police and paramilitary personnel have been killed.

Does the vote hold with an incomplete assembly?

Mughal, the chief election commissioner, says it does.

“The absence of those legislators actually does not matter,” he said. “While morally one may say it is not adequate, but legally and constitutionally, it is no bar and elections will go ahead tomorrow.”

“The people of Poonch division, particularly in Rawalakot and Sudhanoti, are being subjected to collective punishment for demanding their rights and refusing to surrender to power,” he said. “Excluding them from the electoral process and denying them any meaningful role in forming the government sends a chilling message: Anyone demanding structural reform, accountable government and better public services will be punished.”

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Central Crime Branch (CCB) has arrested Ganesan, a longtime aide of granite businessman and Gem Granites chief Veeramani, in connection
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Central Crime Branch (CCB) has arrested Ganesan, a longtime aide of granite businessman and Gem Granites chief Veeramani, in connection with a POCSO case involving the alleged sexual abuse of minor girls.Ganesan is the fourth accused arrested in the case. Police said he had worked with Veeramani’s Gem Granites for 23 years and is currently employed with Balaji Global Enterprises.According to investigators, Ganesan had video clips on his mobile phone that purportedly showed Veeramani in an obscene act involving a minor girl. Police said he did not inform the authorities about the videos.The CCB is now investigating how Ganesan came to possess the clips and why he allegedly kept them without alerting police. Investigators are also examining his mobile phone to determine whether any data was deleted.What is the Veeramani case?Veeramani was arrested on August 29 along with two alleged accomplices after the Anti-Vice Squad (AVS) registered a case over the alleged rape of minor girls. The three accused were subsequently remanded in Puzhal Central Prison.Police said the case came to light after a USB drive containing a video clip purportedly showing Veeramani sexually assaulting a juvenile girl was recovered. Investigators identified the survivor and established that she was a minor when the alleged offence took place in 2019.The video was also examined as part of the investigation into the allegations against Veeramani.The investigation has also expanded to suspected financial transactions allegedly made to influence the earlier probe, police said.Investigators are examining bank transactions and the possible involvement of intermediaries in the movement of funds.Case takes political turnThe ruling TVK on Wednesday demanded that DMK president MK Stalin explain how the POCSO case involving Veeramani was handled when the DMK was in power, alleging that the investigation was allowed to weaken and questioning why a final report was filed.The TVK alleged that the case had been “buried”. The party also questioned former law minister S. Regupathy over his handling of video footage submitted in connection with the case.“Under whose pressure did the then Law Minister Regupathy allow the investigation to be weakened? articles.title: Afghanistan vows to respond after Pakistani air strikes kill four
articles.summary: Pakistan said it carried out air strikes on 10 locations in Afghanistan used to store and launch drones.
articles.body:
Pakistani air strikes on Afghanistan have killed at least four people, a spokesman for the Afghan Taliban government said, promising to deliver an “appropriate response”.

Pakistan said on Thursday it carried out air strikes on 10 locations in Afghanistan used to store and launch drones, some of which were used in cross-border attacks.

Afghanistan’s Taliban government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said the air strikes targeted Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces.

A resident in Kandahar city told the AFP news agency that an air strike hit the city in southern Afghanistan. The resident said they heard a jet, then a large explosion, followed by a fire in the centre of Kandahar city, AFP reported.

Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said air strikes were “deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan”.

He condemned a “deliberate and unlawful incursion into Pakistan by drones” on Wednesday.

“This constitutes a blatant violation of Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and is a grave and unacceptable act of aggression,” he said.

Taliban officials denied that their government launched drones against Pakistan on Wednesday.

The air raids on Thursday were carried out as tensions grow between the former allies over attacks by armed groups in Pakistan, which triggered their worst fighting in years in February.

Islamabad accuses Kabul of harbouring fighters who stage cross-border attacks, but Afghanistan’s Taliban government denies harbouring anti-Pakistani armed groups and says the attacks are Pakistan’s internal problem.

An attack on a police facility in northwestern Pakistan last week that killed at least 21 people has reignited ⁠fighting between the countries after nearly three months of ⁠relative calm. A Pakistan Taliban faction claimed responsibility for the blast and subsequent gun battle .

On Monday, air raids targeting three locations in northeastern Afghanistan killed three civilians in the Nurgal district of Kunar province, Afghan officials said. Islamabad said it killed 28 “terrorists”.

The escalation threatens mediation efforts by China, Turkiye, Qatar and Saudi Arabia to broker a lasting peace between the two neighbours.

Relations between the former allies have been strained since the fighting in February, the worst for years.

articles.title: 'I can't see it stopping' - Middlesbrough's young men on gangs
articles.summary: Last month's deadly A66 crash shone a light on organised crime and opportunities for young people in Middlesbrough.
articles.body:
Inside Hemlington Boxing Club in Middlesbrough, music is drowned out by the sound of gloves hitting pads.

For young men here, nights in the ring are far better than the alternative.

Because outside, away from the bright lights of the gym, riders wearing balaclavas roar past on quad bikes in the darkness.

"You see it all the time," says Dylan, a 20-year-old who trains at the club.

"But I just can't see it stopping. The police can't really do much against it."

Attention has turned to organised crime in Middlesbrough since seven people, including two police officers, were killed last month in a crash.

A Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by officers travelled the wrong way along the A66 and collided head-on with a police car.

For young men like Dylan, who knew one of the lads killed, there are worries about how easy it is to get sucked into a criminal way of life.

"You could walk around the corner and there's just a gang of lads stood there and they shout you over," he says.

Dylan and other boxers tell BBC Newsbeat they blame a lack of safe activities and opportunities for young people in the area.

He says getting into the sport has kept them away from gangs on the streets.

"It stops you going down these bad tracks of crime, drugs, and what most of the lads my age are doing," he says.

"It's just not something I want to be involved in, really," says Dylan.

"I don't think anyone would, but some people just get forced down these routes."

In a report published last month , the Centre for Social Justice found that north-east England has the highest rate of NEETs in the UK.

About one in five 16 to 24-year olds from the region is not in education, employment or training.

Dylan works as a joiner and says he's lucky to have found a job that "keeps you busy and keeps your brain active".

"I think that's where it's going wrong, because people haven't got anything to do," he says.

"So they go into [crime], and it just spirals from there.

"I wish it would all stop, but it's not going to because no-one's got the answer for it."

Michael Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae and Cole Worthy, both 17, were killed in the crash, as were PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, who were in the police car.

Of the men in the Passat, only Michael Cahill had no convictions. The other four had 30 between them for crimes including car theft, drug possession, assaulting police officers and driving offences.

TikTok posts from an account thought to belong to Makai Saddington had appeared to share this type of content.

Dangerous driving videos 'everywhere' online

Louis, 16, who also trains at Hemlington, says similar clips pop up "everywhere" on his own feeds.

"I've seen quite a few videos on driving cars at high speeds," he says. "I just don't think it's cool."

He says he'd known Theo Rae since the two were at primary school, and was shocked by news of the fatal crash.

Louis says the boxing gym gives him somewhere safe to spend his time, instead of chasing an adrenaline rush from breaking the law.

He wants more people to have access to "sports, or something they enjoy which isn't doing dangerous stuff".

'Everyone in my family says get out of Middlesbrough'

Alex, 21, has been training at Hemlington for just over two years.

"If I wasn't here I'd just be out with my mates, or I'd just be sat at home doing nothing," he says.

For Alex, it's not hard to see how others end up spending their time out in the streets.

"Realistically, what are you going to do on a night?" he says.

"There's nothing to do. Everyone's just out and about, especially the kids."

Alex says crime has become "normal" in the area.

"People find it a game almost, recording things for TikTok. It's a 'catch me if you can'."

Since the A66 crash, Alex says, his family has been telling him to "get out" of the area.

"You hear nothing good from Middlesbrough any more," he says.

"I wouldn't want to bring my kids up round here with all the stuff that's going on".

'It's difficult, but you're going to have to trust police'

James, 24, who recently moved away to Peterlee, about an hour's bus ride north, says he used to see "quite a lot" of gang activity.

"It might be drugs or knife crime or little petty things," he says.

Cleveland Police has been criticised since the crash, and some residents previously told the BBC they'd "rather die" than dial 999 because their trust in the force was so low.

James and the other boxers who speak to Newsbeat take a more balanced view when it comes to the police, but agree more work is needed to improve relations.

The authorities need to "get to know the people more, understand the people more" to build trust, says James.

"I think the moment you relate to people, that's the moment you've opened the door to getting people's trust."

Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller tells Newsbeat the aftermath of the A66 crash has been hard for the force, with "an incredible amount of grief" for the two officers who died.

But, she says, the local area has been "portrayed in the national media in a way that we don't necessarily recognise".

"We appreciate there are issues here. We know that there are things that policing needs to do, others need to do to make this area feel safer and be safer," she says.

Fuller says a "minority" intent on causing harm "can have a real disproportionate impact on communities" and encouraged people to report problems.

She says the area should "be grateful" for lads like those at the boxing gym who'd chosen to "walk away" and not get involved in crime.

"We hope that people will look out for each other, spot signs of when people are getting drawn into crime and report it to us so that we can help people."

articles.title: Australian homeowner blamed six neighbouring trees for damage to her 130-year-old heritage home and sought $23,650.86 for repairs; NSW court rejected the claim after finding no proven link to the trees
articles.summary: An Australian homeowner who blamed six trees on neighbouring property for damage to her 130-year-old heritage home has failed in her claim for tree
articles.body: An Australian homeowner who blamed six trees on neighbouring property for damage to her 130-year-old heritage home has failed in her claim for tree removal and about $23,650 in repair costs. The NSW Land and Environment Court found that there was not enough evidence to establish that the trees had caused, were causing, or were likely to cause damage to her property, Legal 500 reported last week.Catherine Armstrong, who owns a heritage-listed home in Cremorne, NSW, had alleged that six trees on the adjoining property were responsible for several problems at her house. These included cracks in sandstone walls, internal cracking, movement of the front verandah, failure of a retaining wall and damage to a boundary fence. She brought the case against the Owners of Strata Plan 5548, which owns the neighbouring apartment complex.Armstrong sought orders under Part 2 of the Trees (Disputes Between Neighbours) Act 2006 (NSW). Her application sought the removal of the six trees and stump grinding, about $23,650.86 for repairs, remedial work on the neighbouring property and restoration work on her own home. She relied mainly on arboricultural and engineering evidence, which suggested that tree roots and abnormal moisture conditions were contributing to structural movement and cracking.The Court accepted that damage to the property existed. However, it found that the evidence did not establish the required link between the particular trees and the damage claimed by Armstrong. The case, Armstrong v The Owners of Strata Plan 5548 NSWLEC 1611, was decided by the NSW Land and Environment Court.Reason for court's rejectionThe Court said Armstrong had to establish, on the balance of probabilities, that the trees had caused, were causing, or were likely in the near future to cause damage. Simply showing that trees were close to a damaged property was not enough.The engineering evidence identified several possible causes of the damage. But the Commissioner found that identifying possibilities did not prove that the trees were responsible. The Court also noted that four of the trees had already been removed following earlier complaints.Also, excavation carried out in 2022 did not find roots near the damaged areas at the front of the property. Roots were found near the rear extension, but they were not close to the cracked sandstone wall, which formed a significant part of Armstrong's claim.The court also noted that no root mapping, tracing, microscopic examination or similar testing had been carried out to establish that roots from the six trees were responsible for the structural movement or damage.Other causes pointed outThe evidence, according to the court, pointed more strongly towards abnormal moisture conditions than tree-related damage. The case material identified several possible factors, including a raised garden bed, watering system, leaking gutter, drainage and moisture conditions, clay soil and structural effects linked to a later second-storey addition.The court found that the mounded garden bed and abnormal moisture conditions were affecting the fence and sandstone wall. It also accepted that maintenance and repair work was needed to protect the heritage building.However, those findings did not give the court a basis to order the removal of the trees. The Commissioner also was not persuaded that decaying roots from trees that had already been removed would create voids and lead to future damage.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Harry Potter play producer says cost of living made two-part show 'impossible'
articles.summary: The London production, which has been running for 10 years, will reopen next month as a one-part show.
articles.body:
A Harry Potter And The Cursed Child producer has said the rising cost of living made it "literally impossible" to retain the play's original format in two parts.

The production has been cut down to a single three-hour show and is set to re-open in the West End next month.

"The cost of living has gone up 30-40% since the pandemic, including running shows," producer Sonia Friedman said in comments reported by media at a launch event. "The only way we could continue to run it as a two-parter would be by charging an amount for the tickets that would be unaffordable and inaccessible."

The two-part play, a sequel to JK Rowling's books, premiered in the West End in 2016 and closed on 20 September.

The changes to the West End production follow the 2021 relaunch of the play as a single show on Broadway in New York City.

"The pandemic, the cost of living and the wars going on around the world accelerated that decision in New York, and that's where we are now with London," Friedman said.

"Of course we'll miss it but it was absolutely the right call and we've got a beautiful alternate version that we're very proud of."

Director John Tiffany said at the launch event that he and writer Jack Thorne - who also wrote acclaimed Netflix series Adolescence - had to be "dragged, kicking and screaming to make the one-parter" due to the success of their original script, the Times reported.

However, Tiffany said the new version meant "more people are going to get to see this show and not have to pay a fortune for it", according to The Stage.

The play takes place 19 years after the final book and follows Harry's son Albus Severus as he arrives at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

The production has been seen by more than 14 million people around the world, including over 2.5 million in London.

The reimagined one-part production will retain some of its original cast, including David Ricardo-Pearce as Harry Potter, Thomas Aldridge as Ron Weasley and Naana Agyei Ampadu as Hermione Granger.

New actors have been cast in the roles of Albus Potter, Ginny Potter, Rose Granger-Weasley, Draco Malfoy and Scorpius Malfoy.

articles.summary: JHAJJAR: Gangster Mainpal Badli alias Mainpal Dhilla arrived at a farmhouse in Jhajjar under heavy police security on Wednesday to marry his Cambodian
articles.body: JHAJJAR: Gangster Mainpal Badli alias Mainpal Dhilla arrived at a farmhouse in Jhajjar under heavy police security on Wednesday to marry his Cambodian partner after a court granted him 12-hour custody parole.Badli, who is serving a life sentence in jail, was brought out of custody at 8am and has been allowed to remain out until 8pm on September 24. He will remain under police surveillance throughout the parole period and will be taken back to jail after the wedding.The wedding is being held at Dulina Farm on the Jhajjar-Gurugram Road, near the jail. His partner, a Cambodian national, has arrived in Jhajjar with her family and three children. The wedding rituals are being performed according to Hindu customs.From life sentence to Cambodia and backMainpal Dhilla, a native of Badli village in Jhajjar district, was arrested last year after being extradited from Cambodia in an operation coordinated by the CBI, Haryana Police and the Union ministries of home and external affairs.According to officials, Dhilla has 22 cases registered against him, including murder. He was convicted in three cases registered in 2007 and 2010 and was serving a life sentence at Hisar jail.Dhilla had earlier been released on parole on July 17, 2018, but allegedly fled the country on August 29 that year using a fake identity, officials said. He subsequently travelled to Cambodia and established a base in Siem Reap, where he reportedly ran a nightclub and married a local woman, with whom he had three children.Extradited from CambodiaFollowing a request from Haryana Police, the CBI obtained an Interpol Red Notice against Dhilla on November 6, 2024. Investigators traced his movements from Thailand to Cambodia and informed Cambodian authorities that he was allegedly travelling on fraudulent documents.The CBI subsequently sought his provisional arrest through Interpol channels on March 26, 2025. Cambodian authorities arrested him on July 24, 2025, and later agreed to hand him over to India through diplomatic channels.A Haryana STF team led by IPS officer Wasim Akhtar travelled to Cambodia and brought Dhilla back to India. He was formally arrested after landing at Delhi airport.Dhilla was sentenced to life imprisonment on April 29, 2013, in a Bahadurgarh case involving murder, attempt to murder, illegal use of firearms and criminal conspiracy. articles.title: CEC Gyanesh Kumar: Why India's Election Commission is in the eye of a storm - again
articles.summary: India's polling monitor is facing yet another crisis of credibility with fresh allegations against its chief.
articles.body:
India's Election Commission (ECI) is facing yet another crisis of credibility after a series of fresh allegations of irregularities against its chief.

One of the most trusted public institutions in the world's largest democracy, the three-member commission is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and includes Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as commissioners.

The latest row broke out after a report in the Indian Express newspaper said that in the past few months, CEC Kumar had been repeatedly questioned by his two colleagues over the integrity of the voter database, changes to the way new voters are enrolled and the security of the electoral rolls itself.

The report said that Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi objected to several decisions which were taken without their knowledge. There were at least 14 times in the past 10 months when Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi were kept in the dark, it added.

In one instance, the report says, the two commissioners even wrote a letter complaining to the chief secretary, the top bureaucrat in the Indian government.

The revelations have created a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation. Sandhu and Joshi have not publicly commented on the report but the ECI said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process".

The report comes at a time when the commission is carrying out a controversial country-wide revision of the electoral database.

The Election Commission says the aim of this Special Intensive Revision - better known by its acronym SIR - is to ensure that no ineligible name remains on the rolls.

It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.

But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing CEC Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.

But the latest revelations are being seen as much more serious as they are about questions being raised from within the Election Commission about the way its chief is functioning.

From the start, questions have lingered over the robustness of the revision, which has seen 130 million names from across India struck off the voters' list.

Millions of voters have also complained to the authorities that their names are missing, saying the new process set by SIR to register as voters is too cumbersome and involves furnishing documents that many don't have.

Former CEC SY Quraishi, who says he has "been a critic of the SIR from the beginning", told news agency PTI that he always wondered why Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi had been "keeping quiet".

"[Now] I realised that very silently and quietly they were protesting, they were writing notes. That is a good thing, they have gone up in my esteem," he said.

The revelations have also provided fresh ammunition to the opposition parties and critics who have repeatedly claimed that SIR is being used to exclude their voters for the BJP's benefit and that elections in India are no longer free and fair.

On Wednesday, angry opposition politicians once again questioned the sanctity of India's election process and demanded that CEC Kumar resign, saying he had no right to continue in office, with some even calling for his arrest.

The charge was led by MP and senior Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi who has repeatedly accused the Commission of "stealing votes from the opposition". On Wednesday, he also accused the Commission and its officers of "treason".

"Vote chori [theft] is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our constitution. The BJP, RSS [Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh] and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason. Justice will be served," he posted on X . He also shared a 15-second video telling the commission and its officers that "your time will come. You cannot get away".

Mamata Banerjee, leader of the regional Mamata All India Trinamool Congress, called for Kumar's arrest and demanded fresh polls with the pre-SIR voters' list in the state of West Bengal which she lost to the BJP in the recent elections. At least 2.7million voters were removed in the state during SIR - Banerjee and her supporters say that cost them dozens of seats and the election win.

Within hours of the Indian Express report and statements from opposition leaders, the Election Commission put out a statement defending its way of working.

"Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken.

"Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the statement said.

The note said that highlighting "certain specific internal notes and observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives" give only part of the picture.

And that in recent months, the commission has "introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full commission in the past one year".

The BJP has also defended CEC Kumar, calling the opposition criticism a "smear campaign" and that dissent was "a sign of a vibrant democracy".

Party spokesperson Sambit Patra told a press conference that "ever since the Modi government came to power in 2014, opposition parties have been collapsing one after the other". And because they cannot win elections, they are trying to "undermine the institutions of the country", he said.

But the row over the election database is likely to intensify. Banerjee has already said opposition parties will hold protests until Kumar remains CEC.

And India's influential Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which recently forced the education minister to resign, has also said it will protest against the "hijacking of India's democracy".

Analysts say the defence of the Election Commission is unlikely to satisfy many, with some pointing out that its statement doesn't address all the issues raised in the newspaper report and that "CEC Kumar needs to clear the air if we are to view the Commission as an impartial body".

articles.title: Netanyahu takes UN stage with one eye on Israel’s election
articles.summary: As criticism of Israel intensifies, Israeli PM Netanyahu heads to the UN with his own political future in focus.
articles.body:
When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu takes to his feet at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York later on Thursday, he does so at a critical point in both his political career and in his country’s long and fractious relationship with the international body.

Israel has faced repeated accusations of genocide at the UN, as well as systematic war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Those criticisms continue to shape the country’s fractious relationship with the body.

For Netanyahu, appearing in front of the UNGA for the 15th time, the stakes have rarely been higher. Addressing a domestic Israeli audience that polls show to be losing faith in him and his Likud party in the run-up to crucial elections later this year, Netanyahu has already pitched himself as Israel’s primary voice on the international stage.

Nevertheless, analysts say Netanyahu’s address could prove a pivotal moment domestically, amplified by international criticism of Israel and expected to dominate headlines and be carried live across the country’s television networks.

“This is a regular fixture for him,” former Israeli consul general in New York and ex-government adviser, Alon Pinkas, told Al Jazeera. “It’s his way of being seen in Israel as standing up against the world and of telling members that he will never give up or surrender. He’s also turned the event into some kind of national holiday in Israel, with everyone sitting down to watch the address on television. He’s brainwashed people in Israel into believing his speech is somehow an announcement of policy, stated in defiance of the [rest of the world] who don’t believe a word he says.”

Israeli leaders have long framed their stance towards the UN as one of defiance in the face of hostility. The UN has long been a platform for critics of Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestinian land and repeated attacks on its neighbours. It has included attempts to censure Israel over what UN investigators have described as apartheid in the West Bank, as well as accusations of genocide and pogroms across the occupied Palestinian territory since October 2023.

There have been numerous UNGA resolutions criticising Israel’s conduct – nearly all dismissed by Israeli lawmakers as evidence of institutional bias – culminating in Israel declaring UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres persona non grata and severely restricting the operations of the UN’s agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.

“Generally speaking, many Israelis tend to see the UN as anti-Israeli,” Nimrod Goren, the president of the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies, Mitvim, said.

Against that background, criticism from New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani – already cast as anti-Israel in the Israeli press – has drawn greater public attention to the event. Underscoring the sense of hostility towards Israel are stories within the country’s media suggesting that Netanyahu’s visit to New York has been curtailed due to unspecified security concerns, with the Israeli premier expected to fly out of New York on the same day as his arrival.

In response, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, who has repeatedly accused the organisation of waging “diplomatic terrorism” against the state, called for Mamdani’s arrest for what he said was the mayor’s incitement against New York’s Jewish community before Netanyahu’s visit.

“Netanyahu is going into his UNGA speech with not one but both eyes focused firmly on the upcoming Israeli election,” Goren said. “The speech is usually treated in Israel as a major event, receiving broad coverage and dominating the news cycle. Netanyahu will likely try to leverage this to bolster his image as a close ally of the US and to talk up the threat posed by Iran.”

Some have interpreted US President Donald Trump’s apparent lack of availability to meet Netanyahu during this trip as a sign of waning support. But US backing for Israel at the UN has remained steadfast since the October 7 attack and has contributed to growing frustration within the UN over what they see as Israel’s ability to resist international censure.

Alongside the creation of the Board of Peace, which shifted significant responsibility for Gaza’s future from the UN to the Trump-founded organisation, Washington has repeatedly used its veto at the UN Security Council (UNSC) to shield Israel from resolutions it opposes. The US has vetoed at least six UNSC resolutions on Gaza since October 2023, most of them demanding an immediate ceasefire.

“There seems to be genuine frustration within the UN General Assembly over the body’s failure to play a significant political role in Gaza and the West Bank, but also in its failure to protect its own staff and agencies,” Chatham House Associate Fellow Zizette Darkazally, who previously worked with the UN, said.

“However, it’s worth remembering the context the UN operates within in the occupied territories and the important humanitarian role it plays. The UN continues to get aid and medical support into Gaza and the West Bank, which are both areas where Israel has absolute control over access,” she said. “It’s also worth remembering that the UN is only as strong as the commitment of its member states.

“That, combined with a system of veto that’s more than 80 years old, has left the organisation weaker now than it had ever been,” she said of the confrontations between the UN and Israel. “And we’re seeing the effects of that, not just in Palestine, but in Yemen, Sudan and Iran, where the UN is playing next to no political role.”

articles.title: For 20 years, a Western Australia teacher has paddled a kayak to school; his daily route across Albany Harbour ends at the classroom door
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of Gary Fullarton, a math teacher in Albany, Western Australia, who has been kayaking to school for 20 years. His daily 30-minute paddle across Oyster Harbour not only provides him with exercise but also a serene connection to nature. Learn about his adventures on the water and the environmental benefits of his unique commute.
articles.body: Gary Fullarton has been starting his workday by putting a kayak into Oyster Harbour and paddling toward the school where he teaches mathematics for about 20 years. Fullarton teaches at Great Southern Grammar in Albany, Western Australia. His paddle across the harbour takes about 30 minutes depending on the weather and wind, while on rougher mornings, the trip can stretch to around 40 minutes. The school sits on a 144-acre waterfront campus beside Oyster Harbour, which makes the unusual commute possible in the first place.Fullarton told ABC in March 2022 that the idea started when he first moved to the area and noticed the school across the water. He thought kayaking would be a better way to get to the harbour instead of driving around it. Two decades later, the paddle had become part of his normal working routine. He carries his school clothes and other belongings in a dry bag stored inside the kayak, and a trolley helps him move the boat between his home and the water. Once he reaches the opposite side, he packs up the kayak and walks onto the school grounds.The commute changes with the weatherWind and water conditions determine how long the crossing takes, and Fullarton said lightning is the main weather condition that stops him from kayaking. On calm mornings, the harbour can be almost glass-like. Mist is also common, which gives the journey a very different setting from a conventional drive to work. Fullarton told ABC that he finds the paddle relaxing and considers it a form of exercise that leaves him ready for the school day.Oyster Harbour is a permanently open estuary with seafood and wildlife, which includes commercial oyster and mussel farms. Fullarton has encountered dolphins, seals, stingrays and a shark while crossing the water. On one occasion, a dolphin surfaced close behind his kayak, while on another morning, he caught four fish during the trip and arrived late to class after cleaning them.Great Southern Grammar says that the school’s 144-acre site is located beside Oyster Harbour, about 16 kilometres from Albany, and includes bushland, wetlands and waterfront areas. The school opened in 1999 before moving to its current Lower Kalgan location in 2000. That location is central to Fullarton's commute, since the school is not simply near the water. Its campus occupies a waterfront site, which allows the final stretch of his journey to end close to where he works.From kayak to classroomFullarton has managed to make the crossing without capsizing, although he does not treat the trip as completely predictable. Stronger conditions can slow the journey, while wildlife occasionally appears alongside the boat. Fullarton told ABC that he has occasionally put a fishing lure behind the kayak while paddling. The catch has been inconsistent, but the unusual combination of commuting and fishing has produced at least one memorable morning.Fullarton described the trip as therapeutic and said it provides exercise without leaving him exhausted before teaching begins. He also pointed to fuel costs and the environmental advantages of paddling. Great Southern Grammar describes its current campus as a waterfront school on Menang Noongar boodja, with learning spaces surrounded by natural and built environments. The school currently serves students from Pre-Kindergarten through Year 12.By the time ABC profiled Fullarton's routine in 2022, he had already been making the journey for roughly two decades. His commute had therefore become an established part of how he travelled to work.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Source of anxiety’: Pakistan cracks down before march to free Imran Khan
articles.summary: The government has blocked highways to the capital and set up container barriers in preparation for the PTI protest.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan — The motorway linking Pakistan’s capital with Peshawar, about 180km (110 miles) to the northwest, has been closed to all traffic until further notice, according to a police notification.

So have the highway towards Dera Ismail Khan, the Hazara motorway and the Grand Trunk Road at Attock.

Each carries traffic between Islamabad and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the province governed by the party of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan, whose supporters plan to march on the capital on Sunday, September 27, demanding his release.

The motorway from Lahore, about 375km (235 miles) to the southeast, remains open.

Inside Islamabad, workers have welded shipping containers together and filled them with gravel and sand so they cannot be pushed aside. Several schools and colleges have been told to shut so police brought in from Punjab and Sindh can be housed there.

Police expect the march to draw between 20,000 and 25,000 people, according to local media reports.

While two of the country’s main opposition parties announced marches on the capital this month, only Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has faced measures on this scale.

Jamaat-e-Islami (JI), a religious party, also set out for Islamabad last week to protest against rising fuel prices. On Monday, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif telephoned its leader, Hafiz Naeemur Rehman, and by Tuesday afternoon JI had postponed its march, pending a meeting between the two men.

Instead, Khan’s three sisters , all over the age of 65, have been detained in Lahore and at least six of the party’s legislators in Islamabad, all under a 1960 public order law that allows preventive detention without charge.

PTI says the true figure of those arrested is higher, and that one lawmaker taken from the parliament lodges has not been traced since.

Khan has been in prison since August 2023 and remains Pakistan’s most prominent opposition figure. But his party enters the final stretch before the protest weakened, with no major demonstration outside Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since November 2024, by its own account.

Yet, say analysts, the Pakistani government appears to be treating the protest march as a far bigger threat than a regular political event would warrant.

“While this is undoubtedly a difficult moment for PTI, it is equally exposing the government’s own frustration,” Habib Akram, a Lahore-based political analyst, told Al Jazeera.

“In fact, the government’s conduct suggests something more. It isn’t just afraid of this protest; it has turned this protest into a matter of its own survival.”

More than 2,000 containers have been placed across Islamabad and at Attock Bridge, the main crossing between Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab, according to media reports, with 19,000 police officers on their way from Punjab and Sindh, and thousands more deployed at Attock.

Dawn, the country’s leading English-language newspaper, said in an editorial that the government appeared to be preparing “not for a political event but an invasion”.

Talal Chaudhry, the junior interior minister, rejected the suggestion that the government was shutting down the capital itself.

“Normal life in Islamabad is continuing. Hospitals, offices and essential services are functioning. The containers and security arrangements are precautionary measures, not a shutdown,” he told Al Jazeera.

Rana Ihsaan Afzal, a coordinator to the prime minister and a government spokesperson, was more candid.

“In trying to counter the rhetoric PTI has adopted, we do have to take certain measures, and yes, those measures carry their own consequences too, but we have to look at the bigger picture,” he told Al Jazeera.

It is all being mounted during one of the deadliest weeks for Pakistan’s security forces this year.

An attack on a police compound in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, killed more than 20 people on September 18, and six soldiers were killed in a gunfight in nearby Hangu two days later.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi set those losses against the march in Lahore on Monday.

“The situation in KP [Khyber Pakhtunkhwa] over the past 10 days is before everyone. There was a suicide attack on a mosque, and two or three other attacks. Our captain was killed, our soldiers were killed, our policemen were killed, and these people are preparing to storm a city,” he said.

Government ministers have seized on a remark by Junaid Akbar, PTI’s chief in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, who said protesters would turn Islamabad into Somnath, a Hindu temple in India sacked by Mehmood of Ghazni, an 11th-century invader, to try to paint the upcoming protest as a major law and order threat.

“Peaceful people do not leave their homes carrying nail-studded sticks,” Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said in Kohat on Monday.

But the PTI’s Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, who will lead the September 27 march, answered Tarar in Peshawar on Monday.

“We will go there on nothing but two hands and two feet. There will be nothing else in our hands,” he said.

In a September 18 judgement, the Islamabad High Court ruled that no party could block roads into the capital, and barred provincial governments from using state resources for the march.

Days later came the arrests of Imran Khan’s sisters. Aleema Khan was detained in Lahore on Sunday, and her sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, were taken in a predawn raid on their homes the next day, according to a family statement on September 22.

The Lahore High Court has reserved its decision on whether a petition challenging Aleema’s detention is admissible, after the family’s lawyer argued that the order was issued after the arrest.

Chaudhry said the sisters faced several cases, had led confrontational protests in the past, and were being held as a preventive measure.

PTI says the arrests reach far wider, listing five members of the National Assembly, a senator, provincial legislators and more than 1,500 workers.

“We were peaceful, we are peaceful, and we will remain peaceful. We are being punished for being peaceful,” Gohar Ali Khan, the PTI chairman, said in Peshawar on Monday, noting that four women from Khan’s family, including his wife Bushra Bibi, are now in jail.

‘Long march’ vs ‘permanent plan of action’

But Interior Minister Naqvi suggested that the government is bracing for a confrontation.

“I think this time we will draw up a permanent plan of action. We will not go halfway,” Naqvi said in Lahore on Monday, adding that the matter would be settled “once and for all”.

What he ruled out was a long sit-in of the kind PTI has staged before.

“This time, it will not happen that they come, and the country is shut down for 10 or 20 days. That possibility does not exist,” he said.

Afridi has signalled that he has exactly that in mind.

“The long march is not a T20, it will be a Test match,” he said on Monday, a reference to cricket’s five-day format.

If Naqvi’s comments sound ominous, they also carry a history with them.

On May 9, 2023, after Imran Khan was briefly arrested, his supporters attacked military installations across the country, including burning down a senior commander’s official residence in Lahore. That led to a major crackdown on the PTI’s supporters and leaders, with hundreds placed under arrest for days, and party leaders pressured to leave the group.

Then, on November 26, 2024, a PTI march on Islamabad ended in an overnight crackdown by security forces, in which the party says at least 12 of its supporters were killed. The government denies that, and says four security personnel died — even though Al Jazeera met families of some of the PTI supporters killed.

PTI was stripped of its electoral symbol before the February 2024 general election , forcing its candidates to run as independents.

They still won 93 seats, more than any other party, but could not form a coalition, and the Pakistan Muslim League – Nawaz took power with other major parties.

A Commonwealth observer group, in its report on the polls released a year later, found that decisions by key institutions had “consistently limited the ability of one particular party” to contest the vote, in a reference to the PTI.

While the Election Commission of Pakistan rejected allegations of rigging , two and a half years on, the popularity scale remains tilted in favour of PTI.

Bilal Gilani, executive director of the pollster Gallup Pakistan, said its unpublished Public Opinion Pulse surveys showed a landscape broadly similar to 2024.

“PTI continues to lead nationally, but faces strong competition from PML-N in Punjab and PPP in Sindh,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that Khan remained the country’s most popular leader.

For Akram, that unresolved argument — over the lack of legitimacy of the 2024 election in the eyes of Pakistanis — is what keeps the pressure on.

“You can hold as much power as you want, but that question never fully goes away. It continues to haunt you, and it continues to be a source of anxiety for the government,” Akram said.

In March 2025, army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who now also serves as Pakistan’s chief of defence forces , told a parliamentary security committee that the country must stop acting as a “soft state”.

“How long will we continue to sacrifice countless lives in a manner of a soft state?” he asked, according to state broadcaster PTV.

For Ahmed Ijaz, an Islamabad-based political analyst, the response to the September 27 march is a response to that thinking, rather than the PTI’s strength.

“Behind that confidence lies the thinking of a hard state, one that has decided no one will be granted an unconditional right to protest going forward,” he said.

Akram, however, said that a different factor might also be worrying the government and the military behind it.

The war in the Middle East has pushed petrol to 393.75 rupees ($1.42) a litre ($5.37 per gallon), up about 51 rupees ($0.18) since the start of September. That is what Jamaat-e-Islami was marching against, and it has warned that it will resume its march in October if the prime minister offers no relief.

Akram said the government’s real worry is multiple issues of antigovernment anger — price rises and Imran Khan’s continued incarceration — coming together.

“That merging could then pull other groups out onto the streets too, and that is precisely what worries the government,” he said.

articles.title: Louisville carved this cavern for limestone; now visitors ride underground zip lines and bike through miles of former mine tunnels
articles.summary: Discover the transformed Louisville Mega Cavern, an underground destination for zip line rides, biking, and adventure activities built in a former limestone mine underneath the city.
articles.body: Deep beneath Louisville, Kentucky, a vast underground world stretches beneath roads, businesses and even parts of the Louisville Zoo. What looks from above like an ordinary part of the city is, below ground, a man-made labyrinth created by decades of limestone mining. Today, the Louisville Mega Cavern has been transformed into an unusual destination where visitors can zip through darkness, tackle an aerial ropes course and travel through passages that once echoed with the sound of mining machinery.According to Louisville Mega Cavern, the underground complex covers approximately 100 acres and contains more than four million square feet of space. The cavern extends beneath Louisville, with sections located roughly 75 to 100 feet below the surface. Its sheer scale has also led to the site being described as one of the largest man-made cavern systems in the United States.From limestone quarry to underground giantThe story began in the 1930s, when businessman Ralph Rogers formed Louisville Crushed Stone. The company used the room-and-pillar method of mining, which involved drilling holes and blasting away limestone, leaving behind large pillars of rock that held up the roof. Mining continued from the 1930s until the early 1970s, producing vast amounts of limestone used in construction.The scale of the excavation is difficult to picture. As noted by Mega Cavern, enough rock was removed to build a four-lane highway stretching 357 miles, leaving behind a vast network of underground chambers and passages. The geology of the region made such large-scale excavation possible. Once mining ended, the cavern was far from finished. In 1989, private companies bought the place and started searching for opportunities to give new life to this vast underground cavity.A playground beneath LouisvilleTourism later became part of the cavern’s story. First, there came the tram tour, then more exciting experiences such as the adventure activities that took advantage of the unique size and stability of the cavern. Some of its most popular tourist attractions are the Mega Ziplines. The existing course features six zipline elements, including a duelling zip line as well as two bridge elements. The experience takes up to two and a half hours and includes an adventure course with an explanation of the history of mining in this area as well as its geology. The temperature in the cavern stays constant, at 58°F to 60°F, or about 14–16°C.The cavern also hosts Mega Quest, an underground aerial ropes course with 76 obstacles. Participants move across the platforms and obstacles using climbing gear, turning the former mine into an underground adventure park. The most unique project is the Mega Underground Bike Park. This opened in 2015, and the 320,000-square-foot park features more than 45 trails. Riders could ride underground without worrying about rain, snow or frozen ground, while the vast mined-out chambers gave them plenty of space to jump and ride along dirt trails.More than an attractionHowever, the new life of the Mega Cavern does not stop at tourism alone. Storage facilities continue to operate within this underground structure, benefiting from its secure location and constant temperature. In addition, the cavern hosts “Lights Under Louisville” each year, creating an underground path lit with Christmas lights.The unusual blend of production, storage, and recreation makes the Mega Cavern unique even for the Louisville area. On the surface, traffic passes through an active American city, but below the surface is a land that was intentionally formed from ancient limestone rock. This quarry has been transformed into a striking example of industrial reuse. The stone may be gone, but what remains is a place that has been repurposed as both a museum and a workplace underground.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Florida couple recounts 'miraculous' rescue after surviving harrowing lightning strike during evening stroll
articles.summary: Police bodycam video captured the frantic response after Aaron and Clare Walenga were struck on a popular trail in Winter Haven.
articles.body: A Florida couple said they experienced nothing short of a miracle earlier this month when a bolt of lightning suddenly struck them during an evening stroll and sparked a frantic rescue by several good Samaritans whose heroism was caught on camera. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Aaron Walenga, 48, and his wife, Clare, 43, recounted the harrowing moment in Winter Haven that left Aaron disoriented and paralyzed on the ground, police bodycam video shows, as bystanders rushed in to perform lifesaving measures on his unconscious wife. "I couldn't move the way I wanted to," Aaron said. "I'm trying to get up. I am trying to get to Clare … I'm trying to talk, and I'm not really able to." Aaron and Clare said the incident happened Sept. 2, after the couple dropped off their three children at a weekly church youth group gathering. DASHCAM CAPTURES TERRIFYING MOMENT LIGHTNING NEARLY STRIKES UTAH TRUCK DRIVER "We dropped our kids off at church, and we use that as our date night, and we looked forward to it," he said. "So we went out and had dinner and then, we love to go for a walk." As they walked hand in hand along the popular West Orange Trail, a nearby storm quickly rolled in and a bolt of lightning struck the couple without warning. The next thing Aaron remembers was waking up in severe pain and confused. "My first thought was that we got hit by a car," he said. "I thought maybe a car just ran us over from behind because getting struck by lightning is nothing that would even enter our minds," Aaron said. MONTANA TEEN THROWS LASSO TO MAN IN YELLOWSTONE RIVER IN SPLIT-SECOND RESCUE While still disoriented, Aaron said he saw bystanders and first responders tending to his unresponsive wife. Four good Samaritans had apparently rushed to the scene, immediately calling 911 and performing CPR on Clare before responders arrived roughly 10 minutes later, the couple said. Witnesses told Clare that she had turned blue and stopped breathing for three to four minutes. "I like to talk about the amount of bravery that they showed… they could see the fence beside them that lit up," Aaron said. "It was a big moment to turn around and then go, 'Hey, I think we need to go that direction.' And they did." A hospital visit revealed that Aaron suffered fractured eye sockets, a broken nose, damaged teeth, facial cuts and burns on his hand and wrists, where he was holding an umbrella and wearing an Apple Watch. Despite undergoing a traumatic event, Aaron and Clare described their recovery as "miraculous," noting that they suffered serious conditions, including brain bleeds and heart damage, that they said completely healed within two days. "We're just seeing miracle after miracle and just too many divine things in this unfortunate circumstance to not be noted," Clare said. "We both had brain bleeds, and then I also suffered heart damage. And then when they followed up again two days later, it was healed. Neither of us had any brain bleed damage and my heart situation completely healed," she added. Clare, who suffered intermittent memory loss, regained her full memory roughly two days later. "God's not done with me yet," Clare said, adding that she feels immense gratitude to be alive. DR. MARC SIEGEL: 'THE ANGELS AMONG US' -- A DYING WOMAN, THE SHOFAR AND THE MIRACLE THAT FOLLOWED Since the incident, the family said they have built a strong relationship with the good Samaritans who stepped in that day, adding that they are even planning to return to the trail in a few weeks. The couple said they are overwhelmed by the support they have received from their local church, neighborhood and school communities. Their pastor also helped bring their children safely home on the night of the lightning strike. "Our neighbors are taking care of our yard and our pool for us, so it's just so many things happening without us even asking," Aaron said. "It's very humbling to know that people out there really care for you, and to see the church the way it's supposed to be, where it's not just in a building. It's really the people that are around you, and it's been amazing to watch." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Throughout the ordeal, the couple said they never felt hopeless, crediting their faith for helping them through the shocking experience. "We've never asked ‘Why me?’" Aaron said. "We never got upset, we never felt hopeless. We really felt like even though it was a hard situation… God's been with us and there's a purpose behind it."

articles.title: Some Florida gas stations are charging more than $5 a gallon as the statewide average reaches $4.29; one DeLand station listed regular at $5.39 cash and $5.49 for customers paying by card
articles.summary: Drivers in Florida are paying more at the pump as petrol prices continue to climb, with some stations already charging more than $5 a gallon for regular
articles.body: Drivers in Florida are paying more at the pump as petrol prices continue to climb, with some stations already charging more than $5 a gallon for regular gas. On Wednesday, September 23, gas prices at a Delray Beach Shell station hit $5.19 a gallon, Reuters reported. Some rural stations are charging even more.The statewide average reached $4.29 a gallon on Wednesday, the highest since May, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). Prices continue to rise. One DeLand station off Interstate 4 was charging $5.39 for regular gas for those who pay in cash, and $5.49 for credit card users. Its premium blend, Amoco Ultimate, now costs $6.19 a gallon in cash and $6.29 by credit card. In Miami Beach, a Shell at 508 Arthur Godfrey Road hit $5.59, while a nearby Chevron sat at $5.09. Fort Lauderdale and Delray Beach reported similarly steep prices at major chains.What’s causing the surge?The latest increase in gas prices in Florida, and nationwide, is being driven by a sharp rise in global oil prices. Escalating tensions between the United States and Iran, including attacks affecting tankers and other energy infrastructure, have disrupted or restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and increased fears of supply shortages, The Daytona Beach News-Journal reported.The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints, with about 20 million barrels of oil and petroleum products passing through it each day, accounting for roughly 25% of the world’s seaborne oil trade.Restrictions on shipping through the Strait have raised concerns about how much oil can reach global markets. This matters because crude oil is the biggest component of petrol and diesel prices, and global supply and demand influence wholesale prices, pushing up costs for motorists in Florida and across the US.Several Florida stations are already selling gas for more than $5The $5 threshold is no longer limited to one unusually expensive station. The mobile app GasBuddy listings on Wednesday showed several Florida stations selling regular gasoline above $5 a gallon. In Miami Beach, a Shell station at 508 Arthur Godfrey Road was listed at $5.59 a gallon, while a Chevron at 1453 Alton Road was charging $5.09.In Fort Lauderdale, one Shell station at 1420 East Sunrise Boulevard was listed at $5.27 a gallon. In Delray Beach, a Mobil station at 8081 Congress Avenue was selling regular gasoline for $5.04 a gallon, according to GasBuddy. The app reports gas prices at individual stations across the nation, based on motorists’ reports.Meanwhile, the BP station in DeLand was not included in the GasBuddy listings. The station is known for charging significantly more than the average price in the Daytona Beach and Volusia County area.In Florida, gas prices are rising sharply. On Wednesday, the statewide average reached $4.29 a gallon, up five cents from $4.24 the previous day, AAA Auto Club said. This organisation reports average prices for gasoline and diesel for metro areas, cities, counties and states across the country each morning, based on its comprehensive survey of the final credit card purchases for fuel the night before.As of September 23, Florida’s average price for regular gas was 10 cents higher than a week ago, 43 cents higher than a month ago and $1.23 higher than a year ago, AAA said.Florida has not yet reached its all-time record for regular gasoline. The state's highest statewide average was in June 2022, at $4.89 a gallon. This was during the early months of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The highest national record was $5.01, which was set in June 2022. At $4.29, Florida's current average is 60 cents below that record. However, as individual stations have already surpassed $5, it indicates how prices can differ from the statewide average.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Buddhist deity sculpture bought for about $75 at a garage sale later sold for $2.06 million at auction
articles.summary: A Buddhist sculpture bought at a garage sale for approximately $75–100 later became the centre of a major Sotheby’s auction result, selling for $2.06
articles.body: A Buddhist sculpture bought at a garage sale for approximately $75–100 later became the centre of a major Sotheby’s auction result, selling for $2.06 million in New York. The gilt-bronze figure depicts Cintamanicakra Avalokiteshvara, a form of the Chinese Buddhist deity Avalokiteshvara, also known as Guanyin. According to Sotheby's, the work dates to the late Tang Dynasty / Five Dynasties, and its seller said they had purchased it about 20 years earlier before taking it to an Antiques Roadshow appraisal event in St. Louis. The sculpture entered Sotheby’s Important Chinese Art auction with a pre-sale estimate of $60,000–80,000.Who was Avalokiteshvara, the Buddhist deity behind the $2.06 million sculptureSotheby’s described Avalokiteshvara as “perhaps the most popular and well-known Buddhist deity in China”. The auction house explained that the deity, also known as Guanyin, appears in several forms, including Ekadashamuka, Amogopasha, Shadakshari, Water Moon Guanyin and the less common Cintamanicakra. These different forms developed as Buddhism evolved in China through the transmission and translation of different sutras.The Cintamanicakra form is depicted with six arms. According to Sotheby’s, the figure holds a wish-granting jewel, known as the cintamani, in front of the chest, a chakra or dharma wheel in a raised palm, and a lotus stem in another hand. Another hand holds a mala, while the sixth is planted down for support.Seven-minute bidding battle at Sotheby’s New YorkThe sculpture appeared in Sotheby’s New York auction of Important Chinese Art on 20 March 2019. The auction formed part of Sotheby’s Asia Week sales series, which featured Chinese works of art during the March 2019 auctions.Sotheby’s said the sculpture’s sale followed a “seven-minute bidding battle”. The auction house reported that it had been brought to auction with an estimate of $60,000–80,000, before ultimately selling for $2,060,000. The auction result was listed alongside other Chinese works offered during the Important Chinese Art sale.A Qing Dynasty jade brushpot also sold for $2.06 millionThe Cintamanicakra Avalokiteshvara was one of several notable results from Sotheby’s March 2019 Asia Week sales in New York. The Important Chinese Art auction also included an exceedingly rare and important complete set of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment by the Qianlong Emperor, dated to 1746, which sold for $2.66 million.Another major result was a rare white jade “Imperial Procession” brushpot from the Qing Dynasty (Qianlong/Jiaqing period), which sold for $2.06 million. Sotheby’s also reported that a group of Chinese jade offered by The Art Institute of Chicago sold out, bringing in $3.2 million.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Mary Harvey says she was drugged at an Ole Miss bar and found passed out in her dorm hallway, as kratom was recovered near two student deaths.
articles.body: OXFORD, Miss. – An Ole Miss student says she was drugged at a bar over the weekend, days before two students were found dead, as bars around Oxford tighten security with fears running rampant through the college town. Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said in a news release that investigators are looking into the deaths of two college-aged individuals whose bodies were discovered at separate locations. Authorities have not established a connection between the deaths, though packaged kratom purchased from a retail store was recovered in each investigation. "We do not have confirmed information indicating that kratom or any other substance was a contributing factor in either death," the agency said. WHAT IS KRATOM? RISKS OF POPULAR SUBSTANCE REVEALED AFTER COLLEGE STUDENTS' DEATHS Ole Miss student Mary Harvey told Fox News Digital that she went out to the bars on Saturday night to watch the Rebels' football game against Louisiana State University, where she says she was drugged and couldn't recall much of what happened that night. "Later into that night, around the time when the game ended, I do not remember a single thing. And I was told by a boy that was there that I fell down," Harvey said. TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS Harvey said police put her in an Uber where she was taken to her dorm, where other students needed to help her get to her room. "Later after that, my roommate got in the shower, and she said while she was in the shower, I went missing. And she left the dorm to find me and was searching everywhere, searched every floor. But on her way back from searching, she found me passed out in the hall of my dorm," Harvey said. STUDENTS AT TOP PARTY COLLEGE ON EDGE AFTER RAPE, STRANGULATION REPORTED IN CAMPUS HOUSING Harvey says she no longer feels "safe in my dorm building." She said on Facebook that "people are scared to leave their dorm rooms." "I feel like everything is just kind of getting swept under the rug and covered up when it should be addressed like immediately," she said. Ole Miss student Kenneth Tonos, who works security for several fraternities and sororities on campus, told Fox News Digital that at least three Greek life events have been canceled following the two students' deaths. Tonos said bars are also taking more precautions, with some tightening their screening to track exactly what people bring in. POLICE AT UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA, BERKELEY INVESTIGATE 2 DEAD MEN FOUND ON CAMPUS A spokesman for the University of Mississippi told Fox News Digital that both of the deceased were students there. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Law enforcement is treating the deaths as two separate investigations, and officials have not confirmed whether any substance contributed to either death. Both of the students were males, the county's coroner's office told Fox News on Wednesday. The younger victim died in a dorm room and was 18, while the other died in an off-campus home and was 20. The coroner's office said their names aren't being released yet and noted that toxicology reports are pending and could take weeks. We are also working closely with the families involved and ask that their privacy be respected during an incredibly difficult time," Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said.
