articles.title: Our son’s miracle is a testament to prayer and Fulton Sheen’s intercession
articles.summary: When Sheen is beatified on September 24, James, accompanied by my husband, me and our other seven children, will carry and present the first-class relic at the ceremony
articles.body: Sixteen years ago, in the middle of the night, in the heart of Illinois, a miracle happened. It didn’t begin as a miracle, of course. The chain of events that would end with a miracle of biblical proportions started with me, laboring at home in the arms of my husband. Unbeknownst to us, our healthy baby boy had a knot in his umbilical cord. That knot tightened during his delivery, cutting off his oxygen supply. When the midwife caught him and placed him in my arms, he was stillborn. For the brief moments I held him, he didn’t cry. He didn’t breathe. He had no pulse. Our son, James Fulton, was taken from my arms and placed on the floor. My midwife and her assistant began CPR. My husband performed an emergency baptism, invoking the saints James was named after. Sitting on the floor, I felt like I was falling out of control. COLTON BURPO DESCRIBES MEETING JESUS AND HEARING ANGELS SING DURING NEAR-DEATH EXPERIENCE In my head, I repeated the name of my baby’s namesake, the late Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen — a Catholic televangelist who converted over 50,000 people during his lifetime and who boasted over 30 million weekly viewers for his Emmy-winning show, Life is Worth Living, which aired in the 1950s. In my moment of desperation, my heart and voice continuously called on Sheen to pray for me. I had no idea how profoundly this prayer would change my life — and the lives of millions of Catholics across America, if not the world. After 20 minutes, an ambulance arrived and took James and my husband to the hospital about 20 minutes away. My husband watched in shock as our tiny son — his cold, blue body hooked up to a heart monitor — lay lifeless and pulseless while every method to restart his heart failed. In a separate ambulance, headed to labor and delivery monitoring, I desperately prayed for the son I just wanted to love and hold. After 20 more minutes, the doctors and nurses finally stopped trying to resuscitate him and were seconds from calling the time of death. 'BLIND SIDE' STAR QUINTON AARON SAYS HE 'SAW JESUS' WHILE IN A COMA AFTER NEAR-FATAL STROKE At that moment, when all attempts had ended, James’ heart started to beat. He had been without a pulse for sixty-one minutes. Even then, everyone feared massive organ failure. The doctors stabilized James and transferred him to the NICU. We were warned that if James lived, his life would be filled with limitations and hardships. We prepared our hearts to love James no matter what. We also prayed for Sheen’s intercession for a miracle. During my pregnancy, we had decided to name James after Sheen and asked for his prayer over the life of our son. It was natural, therefore, to continue to call on him, to ask him to pray without ceasing for our sweet baby James. NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD It took years for the extent of James’ miracle to reveal itself. An MRI at three months showed zero brain damage. As he hit milestone after milestone, it was clear that God had truly restored our son. Independent medical professionals additionally confirmed that there was no medical explanation for James’ survival — let alone the fact that he doesn’t have any complications to this day. I knew in that moment that Sheen had interceded for me and my baby boy. I had no idea then, however, that our little miracle could help Sheen too. Years before, in 2002, Bishop Daniel Jenky opened the cause for canonization for Sheen in his hometown of Peoria. For those who don’t know, Catholic canonizations are multiyear processes the Church undergoes to determine whether an individual is officially a Catholic saint. It involves three stages, the data collection stage before someone is declared venerable, an investigation and miracle to declare someone blessed and a second miracle to declare them a saint. For the past 24 years, Catholics involved in Sheen’s canonization efforts have heavily scrutinized his life and works to ensure he merits the titles of "Venerable," "Blessed," and "Saint." In 2012, the Catholic Church declared Sheen "Venerable" after those responsible for investigating his life concluded that he had demonstrated "heroic virtue." LOST SERMONS FROM ONE OF CHRISTIANITY'S GREATEST SAINTS DISCOVERED AFTER 1,600 YEARS And in 2019, the Catholic Church declared that what happened to my son James was a miracle attributed to Sheen. My son’s first moments of life are the reason that Archbishop Fulton Sheen will be declared "Blessed" in Saint Louis on September 24. Today, James is a handsome teenager, if I do say so myself. He is funny, thoughtful and hardworking. He enjoys music, meteorology and working alongside his dad with the high school football team. He takes his faith seriously and has a personal devotion to Sheen. When Sheen is beatified on September 24, James, accompanied by my husband, me and our other seven children, will carry and present the first-class relic at the ceremony. This honor couldn’t be bestowed on a more grateful family. We hope that sharing James’ story and promoting Sheen’s cause for canonization will inspire more Americans to recognize the glory of God and the beauty of the Catholic faith. Sixteen years ago, in the Heart of Illinois, a miracle happened. People who do not know our family refer to that day as the anniversary of the miracle. articles.title: America's beef supply shrinks as cattle farmer warns 'the numbers are just not here anymore'
articles.summary: U.S. beef production fell roughly 800 million pounds in early 2026 as cattle slaughter numbers declined, pushing farmers like Will Harris toward change.
articles.body: Americans are seeing less beef produced domestically as cattle numbers decline, adding pressure to a market already facing high prices. U.S. commercial beef production totaled about 14.4 billion pounds from January through July 2026, down from roughly 15.2 billion pounds during the same period last year, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) data. The number of cattle commercially slaughtered also declined, falling from about 17.5 million during the first seven months of 2025 to 16.2 million during the same period this year, USDA data shows. NFL LEGEND REVEALS WHY EATING 'REAL FOOD' AFTER RETIREMENT LED HIM TO RAISE HIS OWN BEEF Will Harris, a fourth-generation cattle farmer and owner of White Oak Pastures in Bluffton, Georgia, told Fox News Digital that years of financial pressure have contributed to farmers reducing their herds. "Cattle farmers have for so long not made a profit that they have liquidated their herds, and the numbers are just not here anymore," Harris said. Harris said higher cattle prices have not yet led to the kind of expansion among producers that he has seen during previous cycles. "What's different is the higher prices the farmers are getting is not causing them to go back into business," he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Starting or expanding a cattle operation can require significant investments in land, equipment and livestock, which Harris said can make it difficult for new producers to enter the industry. "There's so much money involved in owning land and equipment and livestock that it's just very hard for a person who is not producing to say, 'I think I'll start a farm,'" he said. Harris also expressed concern about the amount of beef the U.S. imports and what he sees as increasing dependence on foreign supplies. "What is happening is that the United States is becoming a larger and larger net importer of beef," Harris said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES The U.S. both imports and exports beef, with trade patterns influenced by domestic production, consumer demand and global markets, according to USDA data. Harris has experienced a major shift in the way cattle are raised over his decades in the industry. After graduating from the University of Georgia with a degree in animal science in 1976, Harris returned to his family's farm and initially followed conventional farming practices, including the use of chemical fertilizers, antibiotics and growth-promoting technologies. Over time, he said, concerns about the long-term effects of those practices led him to change the way he operated the farm. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "They offered a performance boost in the short run," Harris said. "In the long run, they were literally damaging my land, my farm, my community." The farm now follows what Harris describes as regenerative agriculture, an approach he said is intended to work more closely with natural cycles rather than relying on conventional monoculture practices. For consumers trying to understand how their beef was raised, Harris said labels alone may not always provide all the information. "It's increasingly important that that consumer knows something about the farm that the food is raised on," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Harris encouraged consumers who are interested in how their food is produced to research farms and producers and, when possible, buy closer to home. "I wish that consumers would find a more local producer that they could do business with, they could support to help that guy stay in business," he said. articles.title: In 2013, a Maryland real estate developer and his wife paid $200,000 for a derelict firehouse and spent $800,000, then moved their family into a home that kept its siren
articles.summary: Discover how the Krakovskys reimagined a derelict firehouse in Gaithersburg, Maryland, investing $800,000 to create a unique family home while preserving its historical charm.
articles.body: When Alexander and Jackie Krakovsky bought an old firehouse in Gaithersburg, Maryland, in 2013, they were not looking for a conventional suburban house. The two-storey brick building had once accommodated fire engines and equipment, but by then it had fallen into disrepair. The couple saw something different: a chance to preserve an unusual piece of local architecture while turning it into a home for their family.According to The Washington Post, the Krakovskys paid the city $200,000 for the former fire station and subsequently spent about $800,000 converting it into a residence. By the time they moved in, the building had an open-plan living area, bedrooms, offices, a home gym and an in-law suite. Yet some of the most recognisable reminders of its firefighting past remained, including the original arched bays and, perhaps most strikingly, the firehouse siren.From fire station to family homeThe property in question was located in Kentlands, which is a planned community in Gaithersburg, and it had a rich past that went beyond its appearance. Otis Beall Kent built it in 1961, developing his land into Kentlands before his death. The property featured the 1900-era carriage house and a greenhouse, and it was originally built to accommodate Kent's collection of antique fire engines. The city purchased the property in 1992, and the firehouse was considered a historic property. Many years down the line, the property was in a bad state and required a new use. In 2013, Gaithersburg chose the Krakovskys' project to convert it into a single-family house.This was on the condition of one major thing. The façade should have been left intact, as the owners had much freedom with regard to how they could redesign the interior. In other words, it became the challenge for the family to ensure that the building, which was originally constructed to accommodate fire trucks, could be converted into a comfortable modern house, all while retaining its uniqueness. The work of remodelling was done by architects Craig Moloney of CEM Design and Chris McKee of McKee Construction. This is an especially challenging structural remodelling due to the fact that the first floor was originally subdivided into compartments.Keeping the firehouse characterFormerly occupied by truck bays, these spaces became part of the open living space that comprised kitchen, dining, and sitting areas all within a renovated fire station. In place of concrete walls, steel beams and columns were installed, and the new interior incorporated the use of exposed structure along with wood, brick, and modern materials. Even small details that would connect the house to its past were sought out by the new owners. Among them was the brick staircase to the basement that had been spared from the renovation process. A cautionary sign saying "Caution: low head clearance" hung on the wall in the staircase.Even the heating and utility systems had to be worked into the old structure. Pipes, ducts and electrical wiring were fitted into channels cut into the concrete floors, which were later covered with oak planks. Upstairs, there were three bedrooms, including the master bedroom, as well as an office, a laundry and crafts room, and a gym that could be converted into a library as the family’s needs changed. The renovation was designed to give the rooms some flexibility rather than fixing their purpose permanently. The family also wanted to keep another reminder of the property’s past: the greenhouse. Its glass windows were gone, but the space had already found a new use as a vegetable garden.Why adaptive reuse mattersAccording to research published in Habitat International, adaptive reuse can extend the useful life of heritage buildings while reducing the need for demolition and helping retain the energy already invested in an existing structure. The approach also involves balancing the building's historic character with new social and practical uses.This is a case where the difficulty of these transformations comes through clearly. Preserving a historic structure still requires significant work. Today’s homes need new plumbing, electricity, heating, insulation, and functional spaces, which all have to be accommodated in an already existing building. As a result, the home of the Krakovskys was one that was steeped in history but still managed to provide a completely different future. The fire-engine bays became living spaces, and the greenhouse became a vegetable garden. However, there was one element that still remained: the siren, to make people remember that it was built for emergencies and not for living.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Rolls-Royce signs 'multi-million' engine deal
articles.summary: The order will see 18 engines built and maintained by the company from its Derby aerospace centre.
articles.body:
Rolls-Royce has moved forward with a deal to power a new fleet of Airbus long-haul jets for Philippine Airlines.

The FTSE-100 firm will provide 18 engines for nine new Airbus A350-1000 aircraft in a deal worth "hundreds of millions of pounds".

The agreement, once finalised, also includes a maintenance package, meaning Rolls-Royce will continue servicing and monitoring the engines throughout their operational life, officials said.

The government welcomed the deal, saying it would bring "good quality jobs" to the company's Derby base.

The order was first announced as a memorandum of understanding at the Farnborough International Airshow in July.

At the time, Rob Watson, president of civil airspace at Rolls-Royce, said the company was "proud to continue strengthening our long-standing relationship with Philippine Airlines".

While the deal is described as being worth "hundreds of millions", the precise value has not been confirmed.

Airbus designs and manufactures wings for all its commercial aircraft at its Broughton site in North Wales.

Minister for trade Anas Sarwar said: "This news shows British engineering is flying high with world-class innovation that puts our companies at the front of the pack.

"Building these engines and wings brings good quality jobs to Derby and Broughton, and means UK expertise is at the heart of thousands of flights by one of the fastest-growing airlines around the world."

The engine involved, the Trent XWB-97, can operate using a 50% sustainable aviation fuel blend, with plans for it to run on 100% sustainable aviation fuel in the future.

This order follows Philippine Airlines's previous order for nine Trent XWB-97-powered Airbus A350-1000 in 2023.

articles.title: Florida wildlife crew found a female python curled around a huge nest of eggs; the snake and clutch were removed
articles.summary: A striking clip out of Florida shows a massive invasive female python curled around a mound of eggs, tucked deep in thick ferns.
articles.body: A striking clip out of Florida shows a massive invasive female python curled around a mound of eggs, tucked deep in thick ferns. The footage captured wildlife creator thesnakeaholic documenting the snake's removal after she was found brooding over a hidden nest. The nest turned out to be far more than a spectacle; it represented an entire new wave of predators that could have spread deeper into an already stressed ecosystem had it gone undiscovered.What the viral Florida footage of the female python showsAs reported by The Cool Down, the video shows a large female python coiled tightly in thick ferns, positioned directly over a huge pile of eggs she had been guarding. The creator described finding her "coiled up in the ferns sitting on a huge pile of eggs," capturing the moment before the removal began. Removal crews pulled the snake and her entire clutch from the site together, as part of an active, ongoing effort to track down and eliminate invasive pythons across Florida's vegetation-dense habitats before nests like this one go unnoticed.Removing the entire nest matters more than removing one snakeRemoving a single invasive python protects native wildlife, but removing an entire nest goes further; it stops a whole generation of invasive apex predators from ever being born into the ecosystem. Every clutch left undisturbed represents dozens of future snakes capable of spreading into already-stressed habitats, competing with and preying on native species. By targeting nests directly, removal crews interrupt reproduction at its source rather than chasing individual pythons down one by one after they've already hatched and scattered across the landscape.How this removal compares to other nest operations across the stateThis case fits a broader pattern of nest-focused removal work happening statewide. In the Everglades, removers pulled a clutch of 60 eggs from a separate Burmese python nest, while another operation in the same region removed 431 eggs before they could hatch. Elsewhere, Burmese pythons have been documented becoming fiercely protective around their nests, making removals riskier for the crews involved. These cases together highlight how consistently large, and how consistently hidden, these nests can be.What this means for Florida's larger invasive python problemFlorida's Burmese python population remains one of the state's most persistent invasive-species challenges, with nest removals playing a central role in the response. Scientists have also been developing new data-driven tracking methods aimed at making eradication efforts more efficient statewide. Each successful removal, whether it involves one snake or, as in this case, one snake and her entire clutch, chips away at the broader population before it can multiply further and spread into new areas of Florida's ecosystem.You use AI every day. articles.title: "We know the risk..", she traced 76 missing children across 4 states: Meet Seema Dhaka, the Delhi head constable who earned a historic Delhi Police promotion
articles.summary: In 2020, while the Covid-19 pandemic had disrupted normal life across the country, Delhi Police launched an incentive scheme to encourage officers to
articles.body: In 2020, while the Covid-19 pandemic had disrupted normal life across the country, Delhi Police launched an incentive scheme to encourage officers to trace missing children. Among those who took up the challenge was Head Constable Seema Dhaka of Samaypur Badli Police Station in Delhi's Outer North district. In just two and a half months, she traced 76 missing children, with 56 of them below the age of 14. Her achievement made her the first Delhi Police personnel to receive an out-of-turn promotion under the new scheme.The incentive that pushed the search furtherThe incentive scheme was announced by then Delhi Police Commissioner S N Shrivastava in August 2020. Under the scheme, constables or head constables who recovered at least 50 missing children below the age of 14 within 12 months could be considered for an out-of-turn promotion. At least 15 of those children had to be below eight years old. Officers who traced more than 15 missing children during the same period could also receive the Asadharan Karya Puraskar. Dhaka took the challenge seriously. According to Delhi Police and contemporary reports, she traced 76 children within a span of around two and a half months. The children were not all found in Delhi. Her search took her to different parts of the country, including Punjab, West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and nearby areas such as Ghaziabad, Noida, Panipat and Gurugram.The work was particularly difficult during the lockdown, when public transport and train services were disrupted. Dhaka told NDTV that some families had returned to their hometowns during the pandemic, which meant officers sometimes had to work with limited or changing address information to locate them. She also recalled the emotional impact of the work. "It gave me immense happiness when parents were reunited with the children and they showered blessings on me. Today, as I am promoted, my happiness has doubled," she said.From Delhi to West Bengal in search of childrenSome of the cases required searches far beyond the capital. Delhi Police said Dhaka traced children from states including Punjab and West Bengal. One particularly difficult case involved a seven-year-old boy who had gone missing from his home in 2018 and was eventually traced in West Bengal in October 2020. Reports also highlighted the difficult conditions under which some searches were conducted. In West Bengal, Dhaka and her team travelled during the flood season and used boats to reach areas where a missing child had been traced.For Dhaka, the work was not simply about completing a target. She said she understood the pain of parents who had lost their children and wanted to help bring families back together. "When we join police force, we're aware of the challenges involved, and we're aware of the risk to our lives. That doesn't deter us," she told NDTV. She also credited the people around her for helping her succeed. "Cooperation from family and colleagues" helped her significantly in carrying out the demanding work, she said.A historic promotion for extraordinary workDhaka's efforts resulted in a landmark recognition. In November 2020, she was promoted from Head Constable to Assistant Sub-Inspector, becoming the first Delhi Police personnel to receive an out-of-turn promotion under the missing-children incentive scheme. The achievement was significant not only because of the number of children she traced, but also because of the circumstances in which she worked. The pandemic had created additional challenges for police officers, while families who had moved away from Delhi could be difficult to locate. At the time, Delhi Police officials described her efforts as sincere and painstaking. Commissioner S N Shrivastava publicly congratulated her for recovering children and bringing happiness to their families.Dhaka had joined the Delhi Police in 2006. She was a farmer's daughter from Uttar Pradesh and was also a mother to an eight-year-old son at the time of her promotion. Her story became an example of how persistence, detailed investigation and a strong sense of responsibility can make a difference in missing-child cases. Her achievement ultimately represents more than a career promotion. Behind the figure of 76 are children who had gone missing and families who were waiting for answers. For those families, every successful trace meant something far more important than a police statistic: the return of a child.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: As expected, media mocks Jaxson Dart injury because he dared to introduce Trump on stage
articles.summary: Jaxson Dart's season-ending knee injury sparked calls to sign Colin Kaepernick and mockery tied to his appearance with Trump at a New York event.
articles.body: When New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered a season-ending knee injury this week, we knew there'd be two reactions from the overwhelmingly liberal sports media. First, they'd call for the Giants to sign Colin Kaepernick. They do it whenever an NFL team loses a quarterback, even though Kaepernick has not played professional football in a decade. Second, they'd mock Dart’s injury because he made headlines in May by introducing President Donald Trump at a New York City event. Both reactions materialized almost immediately. DAN LE BATARD DEMANDS THE MEDIA MAKE JAXSON DART 'UNCOMFORTABLE' FOR INTRODUCING TRUMP Sports blogger Mike Florio was the first to urge the Giants to sign Kaepernick. Elsewhere, the usual suspects framed Dart's injury as political karma. "Media types say 'Trump Curse' has struck again," wrote HuffPost in an article referring to Dart as a "Trump admirer." "The f—–g Trump curse strikes again," wrote Tara Setmayer, a former GOP communications director on Capitol Hill and CNN commentator, about Dart’s injury on X. Film and TV critic John Rocha shared a photo of Trump and Dart’s interaction, writing, "Everything he touches, y'all. Everything he touches..." Ron Filipkowski, the partisan editor of the anti-Trump outlet MeidasTouch, claimed he had predicted Dart’s injury after the quarterback appeared with Trump. "This was the moment I decided not to draft Dart in fantasy football. He had no chance this season after the Trump Curse," he wrote above a clip of Dart and Trump. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Other outlets adopted a similar tone. "Jaxson Dart's injury reignites Trump sports curse possibility," joked USA Today. The people making these jokes will insist they are harmless. Perhaps some of them believe that. But they know exactly what they are doing and how their majority anti-Trump audiences will respond. Look at the comments under The Athletic’s report about Dart’s season-ending injury. The comment section resembles a fringe political message board, with readers celebrating the injury, asking whether Dart is "vaxxed" and claiming that he deserves this because he supported Trump. Interestingly, we do not know whether Dart is a Trump supporter. Yes, he introduced Trump at an event. But introducing the sitting president is not, on its face, a political statement. The event also took place in the city where Dart plays quarterback. For all we know, Dart would have accepted the same opportunity if a Democrat were in the White House. Despite what the legacy media tells you, some Americans would welcome the chance to associate with the president regardless of their political views. In fact, we suspect most Americans fall into that category. That said, we can probably deduce that Dart doesn't consider Trump a Nazi. And that is enough for some in the media to call him "MAGA" and poke fun at his injury. There's a trend. In 2020, then-ESPN commentator Mark Jones shared posts mocking 49ers defensive end Nick Bosa after Bosa suffered a serious knee injury. The posts referred to Bosa as "MAGA Bosa" and said he deserved to suffer the injury because he stood during the national anthem. Three years later, former ESPN host Keith Olbermann celebrated when Aaron Rodgers tore his Achilles in the opening minutes of the Jets’ season. "Another #SuddenLisfranc due to failure to vaccinate," Olbermann posted on X. When the Jets wrote that Rodgers’ injury was "Not the way any of us wanted it to go," Olbermann responded: "Define 'any.'" This type of behavior reflects how many Americans suffering from Trump Derangement Syndrome (TDS) react when something awful happens to a Trump voter or someone who does not express open disdain for the president. They genuinely believe that anyone who does not hate Trump as deeply as they do is unworthy and deserves to be punished. Sticking to sports commentators, Jemele Hill immediately denounced Charlie Kirk as a racist days after his murder. Of course, sports injuries are not as serious as death. But they matter. Professional athletes have short careers. Major injuries can derail them, and the consequences are not merely physical. Serious injuries can also take a mental toll. And yet liberal sports fans and media figures abandon common decency whenever an injury allows them to score cheap political points. Only one side openly celebrates injuries in sports.

articles.title: A 97-year-old Bronx movie palace that survived subdivision, closure, restoration, a church era and a 2020 fire is becoming a 4,000-seat performing arts center, New York City's second largest theater
articles.summary: New York City is as much of a historic gaga as it is a modern icon.
articles.body: New York City is as much of a historic gaga as it is a modern icon. For years, the place has been hub to world's dreamers and believers, art and artists and anyone who wants to make something happen. One of the most popular thing about the city is also its landmarks and one of them is all set to return to active service after years of closure.Bronx's historic Loewe's Paradise Theatre, a 97-year-old landmark and one of the original five NYC "wonder theatres" will be back to service as a full Performing Arts Centre. Spearheaded by a new management team that includes theatrical producer Scott Perrin, producer and theater owner Peter Martin, and longtime real estate operator Charles Piazza, the new Paradise Performing Arts Center will mark its transition from a historic movie palace into a dynamic cultural institution dedicated to the Bronx community with a special press preview & community welcome event scheduled for Tuesday, November 10th, 2026.With 4,000 seats the Paradise Performing Arts Centre will be the second-largest theatre in New York after Radio City Music Hall, giving the Bronx a large-scale performing arts venue on the on the Grand Concourse, presenting live stage shows, concerts, stand-up comedy, family shows, dance, film, community and educational events.Architect John Eberson, who designed over 500 theaters considered the Paradise his crown jewel. Now, its restoration is intended to return it as close as possible to the pristine condition and grandeur of the theatre when it first opened in 1929. The Paradise is working with EverGreene Architectural Arts, whose previous restoration work includes the Loew's Kings Theatre in Brooklyn and Loew's Jersey Theatre. Kenn Lubin, whose work includes signage for Broadway productions, is overseeing the restoration of the theater's historic signage, with plans to restore and relight the Paradise and Grand Concourse signs. Irwin Seating Company is working to restore the theater's historic seating. Restoration plans also call for the restoring the original ceiling with stars and moving clouds and also include the addition of a rooftop outdoor performance stage, restaurant, bar, and gift store.The core mission of The Paradise Performing Arts Center is to present artistic voices that reflect the diversity of the Bronx while serving as a center for culture, education, economic development, and neighborhood engagement and expanding access to the arts to the widest possible audience. Programming will include concerts, stand-up comedy, family shows, dance, film and educational events. In addition to its public planning, the ornate lobby of the restored Paradise is also now available to host weddings and corporate events, as well as photo and video shoots.“Every borough of New York City has major performing arts centers except The Bronx, so we've reimagined a magnificent, underused, landmark theater to expand access to the arts to the widest possible audience in one of the most arts-underserved neighborhoods of New York,” said PPAC Executive Director, Scott Perrin. “It's going to take a village to bring this goal to fruition, but we've accomplished the first step, and we invite everyone to join us to achieve all the potential of this worthy vision which will celebrate the arts and uplift the community. I also think we're going to profoundly impact countless young people in The Bronx by giving them access to arts and culture in their neighborhood.""The Paradise theater is one of the most spectacular, atmospheric theaters to have ever been built in the United States. We look forward to restoring the interior and exterior to the magnificent beauty from when it first opened on the Grand Concourse in 1929," added managing director Peter Martin.You use AI every day.
